>>>   single-character allele labels that are included as an
>>> attribute in
>>>   the cross and will be used as labels throughout the program (for
>>>   example, in geno.table, effectplot and plot.pxg).  This required
>>>   numerous small changes throughout the package.
>>>
>>>   The maps used for the results from argmax.geno(), calc.genoprob()
>>>   and sim.geno() are now saved as an attribute on the data they
>>>   create (within the cross object) so that create.map() doesn't have
>>>   to be called repeatedly.
>>>
>>>   Moved the code for simulating genotype data in sim.cross() into C,
>>>   to increase speed, and modified it so that one may simulate under
>>>   Frank Stahl's interference model (which includes the chi-square
>>>   model as a special case).
>>>
>>>   If one includes a phenotype named "id" or "ID", this will be
>>> used in
>>>   top.errorlod(), plot.errorlod(), and plot.geno() as identifiers
>>> for
>>>   the individual.
>>>
>>>

>>
>>
>>

messages.subject: Re: R/qtl version 1.03-14
messages.body_plain:
For a single chromosome you might have enough room to plot names simply using the build-in text command of R.
Using the example from the qtl package :

data(hyper)
hyper <- calc.genoprob(hyper, step=2.5, error.prob=0.01)
out.hk <http://out.hk> <- scanone(hyper, method="hk")
mychr<-1
plot(out.hk <http://out.hk>,chr=mychr, col="blue",incl.markers=T)
text(hyper$geno[[mychr]]$map,y=rep(0,length(hyper$geno[[mychr]]$map)),names(hyper$geno[[mychr]]$map),cex=0.6,srt=90,pos=4,offset=-0.1)

Co-segregating markers names overlaps, but can be edited in powerpoint after a metafile export.
Hope this helps,

JF

messages.body_plain:
The output from a permutation test with scantwo is a matrix with two
columns.

the following:

   apply(myoutput, 2, quantile, 0.95)

test, and
are actively working to produce a procedure that is more sensible.

messages.subject: Re: Model
messages.body_plain:
The results of fitqtl() depend on the multiple imputations created by
sim.geno().
If you run fitqtl() a second time without re-running sim.geno(), you
should get
identical results.  However, if you run sim.geno() again followed by
fitqtl(),
the results will be somewhat different as the imputations are random.

The larger the number of imputations (n.draws in sim.geno), the less
variability
there should be.  If you run sim.geno and fitqtl again and the
results are
very different, you should increase the value of n.draws.

messages.subject: Re: permutation test with mr-imp
messages.body_plain:
If you use scanone with method="mr-imp", all missing data
are replaced with a single imputation.

It's better to do sim.geno (probably with n.draws=128 or so)
and then when you run scanone(), use method="imp".

The problem you were having with method="mr-imp" with the imputations
was a bug.  It'll be fixed in the next version.

karl

messages.subject: Re: memory and scantwo
messages.body_plain:
I understand now...the reason for the memory problem is that
with methods "hk" and "imp", scanone and scantwo now do permutations
in "batch mode".  A batch of permuted phenotypes is created,
and these are analyzed simultaneously using multivariate linear
regression.  With a really large number of individuals, this could
be a memory hog.

I guess we need to add an argument that prevents this from happening...
force the usual approach which would use require less memory but more
computation.

In the meantime, the results of the scantwo permutations is a matrix
with two columns.  You can concatenate those together using rbind().

Also, the permutations with scanone and scantwo are not terribly
complicated, so you could just do things from scratch with something
like the following:

   temp <- mycross
   n.perm <- 1000
   for(i in 1:n.perm) {
     temp$pheno <- temp$pheno[sample(nind(temp)),]
     output <- scantwo(temp, ....)
     [save the interesting bits from the output]
   }

karl
